title: Chapter 103 — Measurement of The Whale’s Skeleton
paragraphs: First of all, I want to give you a detailed, plain account of how big this leviathan is when alive, since we are about to show his skeleton briefly. That account may be useful here.

According to a careful calculation I have made, partly based upon Captain Scoresby's estimate of seventy tons for the largest sized Greenland whale of sixty feet in length, a Sperm Whale of the largest magnitude, between eighty-five and ninety feet in length and something less than forty feet in its fullest circumference, will weigh at least ninety tons. So that, reckoning thirteen men to a ton, he would considerably outweigh the combined population of a whole village of eleven hundred inhabitants.
Don't you think, then, that brains, like yoked cattle, should be put to this leviathan, to make him budge at all in any landsman's imagination?

I have already shown you, in various ways, his skull, spout-hole, jaw, teeth, tail, forehead, fins and several other parts, so now I will simply point out what is most interesting in the general mass of his bones once they are laid bare. But the colossal skull makes up so very large a share of the whole length of the skeleton, and it is by far the most complicated part, and nothing about it will be repeated in this chapter; so you must be sure to keep it in your mind, or under your arm, as we go on. Otherwise you will not get a complete idea of the overall structure we are about to look at.

In length, the Sperm Whale's skeleton at Tranque measured seventy-two feet. So that when fully fleshed out and extended in life, he must have been ninety feet long, for in the whale the skeleton loses about one-fifth in length compared with the living body. Of this seventy-two feet, his skull and jaw comprised some twenty feet, leaving about fifty feet of plain backbone. Attached to this backbone, for something less than a third of its length, was the mighty circular basket of ribs that once enclosed his vital organs.

To me this vast chest with its ivory ribs, and the long, plain spine running far away from it in a straight line, looked a good deal like the hull of a great ship just laid down on the stocks, when only about twenty of her bare bow-ribs have been set in place and the keel, for the moment, is otherwise just a long, unconnected timber.

There were ten ribs on each side. The first, counting from the neck, was nearly six feet long. The second, third and fourth each got longer in turn, up to the high point of the fifth, one of the middle ribs, which measured eight feet and a few inches. From there the remaining ribs grew shorter, until the tenth and last spanned only five feet and a few inches. Their thickness was generally in proportion to their length. The middle ribs had the greatest curve. On some of the Arsacides, ribs like these are used as beams to lay footbridges across small streams.

Looking at these ribs, I was struck once again by the point this book has made in so many ways: the whale's skeleton is by no means a mold of his body as it is when clothed in flesh. The largest of the Tranque ribs, one of the middle ones, sat in the part of the fish that is deepest in life. Now, the greatest depth of this particular whale's body, fully clothed, must have been at least sixteen feet, while the matching rib measured only a little over eight. So this rib gave only half a true idea of how big that part was in the living animal. What's more, for some distance along where I now saw only a bare spine, all of it had once been wrapped in tons of extra bulk in the form of flesh, muscle, blood and bowels. Furthermore, in place of the broad fins I saw here only a few jumbled joints, and in place of the heavy, majestic, but boneless flukes, nothing at all!

How vain and foolish, then, I thought, for timid, untraveled man to try to comprehend this wondrous whale rightly by merely poring over his dead, shrunken skeleton, stretched in this peaceful wood. No. Only in the heart of the quickest perils, only when within the swirling of his angry flukes, only on the profound unbounded sea, can the fully living whale be truly found out.

But the spine. For that, the best way to consider it is with a crane, to pile its bones high up on end. No speedy enterprise. But now that it's done, it looks much like Pompey's Pillar, the ancient column at Alexandria.

There are forty-odd vertebrae altogether, and in the skeleton they are not locked together. Most of them lie like the great knobbed blocks of a Gothic spire, forming solid layers of heavy masonry. The largest, one in the middle, is a little under three feet wide and more than four feet deep. The smallest, where the spine narrows into the tail, is only two inches wide and looks rather like a white billiard ball. I was told there had been even smaller ones, but some little cannibal urchins, the priest's children, had stolen them to play marbles with, and they were lost. So we see that the spine of even the hugest living thing tapers off in the end into simple child's play.
